Steve Ballmer was born on March 24, 1956.
Steve Ballmer was born in Detroit, Michigan, U.S.
Steve Ballmer's father was named Frederic Henry (Fritz Hans) Ballmer.
Frederic Ballmer was from Zuchwil, Switzerland and arrived in the United States in 1948.
Frederic Ballmer died in 2000.
Steve Ballmer's mother was named Beatrice Dworkin.
Beatrice Dworkin was the daughter of Samuel Dworkin.
Samuel Dworkin fled to the United States from Russia in 1914.
Samuel Dworkin became a merchant for a glass store.
Through his mother, Steve Ballmer is a second cousin of actress and comedian Gilda Radner.
Steve Ballmer grew up in Farmington Hills, Michigan.
Steve Ballmer lived in Brussels from 1964 to 1967.
Steve Ballmer attended the International School of Brussels.
Steve Ballmer attended college prep and engineering classes at Lawrence Technological University.
Steve Ballmer graduated as valedictorian from Detroit Country Day School.
Steve Ballmer scored 800 on the mathematical section of the SAT.
Steve Ballmer was a National Merit Scholar.
Steve Ballmer eventually became a member of Detroit Country Day School's board of directors.
Steve Ballmer attended Harvard College.
Steve Ballmer was a manager for the Harvard Crimson football team.
Steve Ballmer was a member of the Fox Club.
Steve Ballmer worked on The Harvard Crimson newspaper and the Harvard Advocate.
Steve Ballmer lived down the hall from Bill Gates at Harvard College.
Steve Ballmer scored highly in the William Lowell Putnam Mathematical Competition.
Steve Ballmer graduated magna cum laude with a Bachelor of Arts in applied mathematics and economics in 1977.
Steve Ballmer worked as an assistant product manager at Procter & Gamble for two years.
Steve Ballmer shared an office with Jeff Immelt at Procter & Gamble.
Jeff Immelt later became CEO of General Electric.
Steve Ballmer started attending the Stanford Graduate School of Business for his MBA in 1980.
Steve Ballmer dropped out of the Stanford Graduate School of Business in 1980 to join Microsoft.
Steve Ballmer joined Microsoft on June 11, 1980.
Steve Ballmer became Microsoft's 30th employee and the first business manager hired by Gates at Microsoft.
Steve Ballmer had a salary of $50,000 plus 10% of the profit he generated when he started at Microsoft in 1980.
Dave Marquardt suggested for Microsoft to reorganize as a corporation instead of a private partnership in 1980.
Ballmer proposed owning 8% of the company in exchange for cancelling the profit-sharing model when Microsoft was reorganized.
Allen initially disagreed with Ballmer's proposal but Gates and Allen reached an agreement when Gates agreed to fund most of Ballmer's 8% stake.
When Microsoft was incorporated in 1981, Ballmer owned 8% of the company.
Ballmer sold 39.3 million Microsoft shares for about $955 million in 2003, reducing his ownership to 4%.
In 2003, Ballmer replaced Microsoft's employee stock options program.
Ballmer headed several Microsoft divisions including operations, operating systems development, and sales and support from the early 1980s until 2000.
In February 1992, Ballmer became Executive Vice President for Sales and Support at Microsoft.
Ballmer led the development of the .NET Framework.
On January 13, 2000, Ballmer was officially named the chief executive officer of Microsoft; he shed the title of president in February 2001.
As CEO, Ballmer handled company finances and daily operations while Gates remained chairman of the board and retained control as chief software architect.
Gates relinquished day-to-day activities when he stepped down as chief software architect in 2006 but stayed on as chairman.
Ballmer required detailed business justification to approve new products after becoming CEO.
In 2005, Ballmer recruited B. Kevin Turner from Walmart to become Microsoft's chief operating officer.
B. Kevin Turner was hired at Microsoft to lead the company's sales, marketing, and services group and instill more process and discipline in operations and salesforce.
Ballmer oversaw a "dramatic shift away from the company's PC-first heritage" since Bill Gates' retirement.
In 2012, Businessweek said that under Ballmer's tenure, Microsoft arguably had the best product lineup in its history.
Ballmer drove Microsoft's "connected computing" strategy with acquisitions such as Skype.
Under Ballmer's tenure, Microsoft's share price stagnated while annual revenue surged from $25 billion to $70 billion.
Net income increased 215% to $23 billion and gross profit of 75 cents on every dollar in sales was double that of Google or IBM.
Ballmer maintained the profitability of existing Windows and Office franchises, fended off threats from competitors such as Linux and other open-source operating systems and Google Docs.
Ballmer built half a dozen new businesses including the data centers division and the Xbox entertainment and devices division ($8.9 billion).
Ballmer constructed the company's $20 billion Enterprise Business consisting of new products and services like Exchange, Windows Server, SQL Server, SharePoint, System Center, and Dynamics CRM.
These diversified product mix helped to offset Microsoft's reliance on PCs and mobile computing devices as it entered the post-PC era.

In April 2013, while Windows Phone 8 and Windows 8 had not managed to increase their market share above single digits, the company increased its profit 19% over the previous quarter in 2012 due to the Microsoft Business Division (including Office 365) and Server and Tools division (cloud services).
Ballmer attracted criticism for failing to capitalize on several new consumer technologies.
In May 2012, hedge fund manager David Einhorn called on Ballmer to step down as CEO of Microsoft.
Ballmer delivered the opening keynote at CES in 2009 for the first time since Bill Gates resigned from day-to-day management at Microsoft.
On June 19, 2012, Ballmer revealed Microsoft's first ever computer device, a tablet called Microsoft Surface at an event held in Hollywood, Los Angeles.
Ballmer announced the company's purchase of Nokia's mobile phone division in September 2013 as his last major acquisition for Microsoft as CEO.
On August 23, 2013, Ballmer announced that he would retire within the next 12 months.
A special committee including Bill Gates decided on the next CEO after Ballmer's retirement.
Ballmer regretted the lack of focus on Windows Mobile in the early 2000s which left Microsoft a distant third in the smartphone market by 2013.
Ballmer attributed the success of iPhones to carrier subsidies despite his earlier statements that they would never sell due to their high price.
Ballmer called the acquisition of Nokia's mobile phone division his "toughest decision" during his tenure as CEO.
Ballmer hosted his last company meeting in September 2013 and stepped down from the company's board of directors in August 2014.
The IRS sued Ballmer, Craig Mundie, Jeff Raikes, Jim Allchin, Orlando Ayala, and David Guenther to compel them to testify in Microsoft's corporate tax audit in December 2014.
In 2015, Ballmer co-founded the Ballmer Group, a philanthropic investment company aimed at helping children achieve economic mobility.
In December 2023, CNN estimated that Ballmer was set to collect $1 billion in dividends from his ongoing ownership of Microsoft stock after an increase in its dividend to $3 per share.
Ballmer was a director of Accenture and a general partner of Accenture SCA from 2001 to 2006.
In 2007, Ballmer said there was no chance that the iPhone would get any significant market share.
Speaking at a conference in NYC in 2009, Ballmer criticized Apple's pricing as challenging for the average person in this economic environment.
In 2015, Ballmer called Microsoft's decision to invest in Apple to save it from bankruptcy in 1997 "the craziest thing we ever did".
Ballmer revisited his iPhone statements in 2016 saying he did not realize that Apple was going to have phone carriers build the cost into the customer's monthly bill.
In July 2000, Ballmer called Linux a "communism" and further claimed it infringed with Microsoft's intellectual property.
In June 2001, Ballmer called Linux a "cancer that attaches itself in an intellectual property sense to everything it touches".

Ballmer used the notion of "viral" licensing terms to express his concern over GNU General Public License (GPL) employed by such software requiring all derivative software be under GPL or compatible license.

In April 2003, Ballmer interrupted a skiing holiday in Switzerland to personally plead with the mayor of Munich not to switch to Linux but failed as Munich switched to LiMux despite his offer of a 35% discount.

In March 2016, Ballmer changed his stance on Linux saying he supports his successor Satya Nadella's open source commitments and maintained that his comments in 2001 were right at the time but times have changed.
In 2005, Microsoft sued Google for hiring Kai-Fu Lee claiming it was a violation of his one-year non-compete clause in his contract.
Mark Lucovsky alleged in a sworn statement to a Washington state court that Ballmer became enraged upon hearing that Lucovsky was about to leave Microsoft for Google and vowed to "kill Google".
Ballmer said during the 2011 Web 2.0 Summit in San Francisco that it is hard for him to be excited about Android phones.
In 2013, Ballmer called Google a "monopoly" that should be pressured from market competition authorities.

On March 6, 2008, Seattle mayor Greg Nickels announced that a local ownership group involving Ballmer made a commitment to invest $150 million in cash toward a proposed renovation of KeyArena and were ready to purchase the Seattle SuperSonics.
However, this initiative failed as the SuperSonics relocated to Oklahoma City where they now play as the Oklahoma City Thunder.
In June 2012, Ballmer was an investor in Chris R. Hansen's proposal to build a new arena in the SoDo neighborhood of Seattle and bring the SuperSonics back to Seattle.

On January 9, 2013, Ballmer and Hansen led a group of investors in an attempt to purchase the Sacramento Kings from the Maloof family and relocate them to Seattle for an estimated $650 million but this also fell through.

Following the Donald Sterling scandal in May 2014, Ballmer was the highest bidder in an attempt to purchase the Los Angeles Clippers for a reported price of $2 billion which was then the second-highest bid for a sports franchise in North American sports history after the $2.15 billion sale of the Los Angeles Dodgers in 2012.
After a California court confirmed the authority of Shelly Sterling to sell the team, it was announced on August 12, 2014 that Ballmer would become the owner of the Los Angeles Clippers.
On September 25, 2014, Ballmer said he would bar the team from using Apple products such as iPads and replace them with Microsoft products.
It has been reported that Ballmer had previously also barred his family from using iPhones.

In March 2020, Ballmer agreed to buy The Forum in Inglewood, California which allowed him to build the Intuit Dome in the nearby area since plans for a new Clippers' arena were opposed by the former owners of The Forum.
In a survey conducted by The Athletic in December 2020, Ballmer was voted the best owner in basketball.
As of October 2023, Bloomberg Billionaires Index estimates his personal wealth at around $115 billion making him the fifth-richest person in the world.
On July 1, 2024, Steve Ballmer surpassed Bill Gates to become the sixth-richest person in the world driven by a 21% rise in Microsoft shares.
Steve Ballmer's net worth is mostly in Microsoft stock at $157.2 billion which exceeded Gates's diversified and heavily donated net worth of $156.7 billion.
In November 12, 2014, Ballmer and his wife Connie donated $50 million to the University of Oregon for scholarships, public health research and advocacy, and external branding/communications.
Connie Ballmer is a University of Oregon alumna and previously was on the institution's board of trustees.
On November 13, 2014, Ballmer provided a gift estimated at $60 million to Harvard University's computer science department allowing it to hire new faculty and increase its national stature.
Ballmer previously donated $10 million to the same department in 1994 in a joint gift with Bill Gates.
In 2022, Ballmer donated $425 million to the University of Oregon to fund a new institute for children's behavioral health.
Ballmer is on the World Chairman's Council of the Jewish National Fund which means he has donated US$1 million or more to the JNF.
Steve Ballmer launched USAFacts.org in 2017, a not-for-profit organization whose goal is to allow people to understand U.S. government revenue, spending and societal impact.
He is reported to have contributed $10 million to fund teams of researchers who populated the website's database with official data.
Steve Ballmer married Connie Snyder in 1990.
They have three sons.
The Ballmers live primarily in Hunts Point, Washington.
They own multiple homes in the Seattle area and a total of 10 properties near Coupeville, Washington as of 2024.
